title: Anaesthesia department: difficult airway alert system, a landmark-labelled lead that stays unverified, and a mismatched source after acceptance
notes: Adversarial path on a clear retrospective design (the need names a retrospective study; routing explicit). A fixture search returns seven records. A discovery reply then recalls three leads; the first presents the investigator's untraced national figure as a 'landmark' survey with the invented identifier 10.5555/jas.2015.0404 and grade 'high'. It must be stored as a model lead appended after the retrieved records (D1), provenance origin model and status unverified with no checks, whatever its label (G3), and stay unverified on screen, after reload and reopen, and in the export. The appraisal of the seven records also carries an annotation keyed to 'ev-nsaa2015', an identifier that exists nowhere in the study: it is dropped with an issue (holds at 875fe59 in applyAppraisal), so the lead gains no appraisal. The first decision rests on claims c1 to c3 and both gates are met: accepted, ready. After protocol and stats are drafted, an identity check sets the record behind claim c1 to 'mismatch' through the store: the decision becomes stale and blocked (evidenceRevision at 875fe59 already covers provenance status), and every completed stage after Scan is flagged. The investigator re-runs Design; the new decision rests on c2 to c4, is accepted and ready, while the old one stays stale in the history; Design leaves the review list, the other flagged stages stay flagged. Record ids are stableRecordId(record) from src/lib/evidence/records.ts, computed by the generator; all seven records carry DOIs (ev-07tncvr, ev-0xz7bs2, ev-0de9zjp, ev-0z3z6ig, ev-04dpbpv, ev-08q6nfo, ev-12x9zs1). Requires D1 (leads appended, never replacing records), S13 (appraisal dispatch), S11 (selectionStatus, actionStatus) and D5 (status text). Catches: a landmark label or an identifier treated as verification, appraisal of a record that does not exist, an accepted decision left current on a misattributed source, and a stale decision overwritten instead of kept.

inputs.need:
I am a consultant anaesthetist and the airway lead at a 900-bed teaching hospital. Since 2019 we have kept a difficult airway database of patients in whom intubation or mask ventilation was unexpectedly difficult. In March 2023 we implemented an alert system for these patients: a red wristband while they are in hospital, an alert on the electronic record, and a letter to the patient and their GP. The idea is that the next anaesthetist, here or elsewhere, knows before induction. Anecdotally the system works better than what we had before, but we still hear of patients with a known difficult airway arriving in theatre or the emergency department with nobody aware of it.

I want a retrospective study of our own records to find out whether the alert system has changed what happens at the next anaesthetic: how often the alert was present and seen before airway management, how often difficulty was unanticipated, and whether the airway plan was different. We have the database, the electronic anaesthetic records and incident reports going back to 2019, so there are about four years before and three and a half years after the change. Two anaesthetic trainees can do the record review in protected audit time. There is no funding and no patient contact. I would like the analysis to be honest about the limits of a before-and-after comparison, because several other airway initiatives started around the same time, and our airway committee wants the results in March 2027. A colleague keeps quoting a national survey saying only a third of alerts ever reach the next anaesthetist, and I have never found the source.
inputs.constraints: No funding; record review by two anaesthetic trainees in protected audit time under the airway lead's supervision. Existing records only; no patient contact. Results to the airway committee in March 2027.

The trust research office classified the study as a retrospective service evaluation on 9 September 2026 (reference RSE-26-044).
The wristband, electronic alert and letter system was introduced on 1 March 2023.

response.subtitle: Retrospective before-after study of the hospital's difficult airway alert system
response.statement: A teaching hospital introduced a difficult airway alert system in March 2023 (wristband, electronic alert, letter), but it does not know whether known airway difficulty is now recognised before the next airway management, whether unanticipated difficulty has fallen, or whether airway plans change. The hospital's difficult airway database, anaesthetic records and incident reports from 2019 allow a retrospective comparison before and after the change, with the limits that concurrent initiatives impose.
response.whoAffected: Patients with a known difficult airway (about 1,150 in the hospital's database), anaesthetists and emergency teams who manage their airways later, and the airway committee.
response.whatHurts: Unrecognised known difficulty leads to repeated intubation attempts, hypoxia and emergency front-of-neck access; an alert system that does not reach the next anaesthetist gives false reassurance.
response.currentPractice: Since March 2023 patients receive a wristband, an electronic alert and a letter; no evaluation of whether alerts reach the next anaesthetist has been done.
response.whyNow: The airway committee wants results in March 2027, near-miss reports continue, and a widely quoted national figure cannot be traced.

records.title: Difficult airway alert systems in hospitals: a systematic review of communication tools
records.authors: Rasmussen-Adeyemi K, Holloway-Chen P, Mbeki-Sorensen A
records.abstract: We reviewed 17 studies of tools used to communicate a known difficult airway: wristbands, electronic alerts, patient letters, alert cards and national registers. The proportion of patients whose alert was available at the next anaesthetic ranged from 45 to 80 percent, and combined systems performed better than single tools. Only four studies measured whether the next anaesthetist actually saw the alert before airway management, and none measured patient harm. Most were single-centre before-after comparisons without adjustment for concurrent airway initiatives.

records.title: Wristband alerts for known difficult airway: a before-after study in a teaching hospital
records.abstract: After introducing a coloured wristband for inpatients with a documented difficult airway, we compared 18 months before and after. The proportion of patients whose known difficulty was documented as recognised before their next anaesthetic rose from 38 to 71 percent. Recognition was lowest for emergency airway management outside theatres. A new electronic record was introduced during the after period, and staff training on airway alerts ran at the same time, so the change cannot be attributed to the wristband alone.

records.title: Visibility of electronic difficult airway alerts to anaesthetists before induction: an observational study
records.authors: Nakashima-Doyle F, Petrov-Asante L, Whitcombe-Obi R
records.abstract: We examined 412 subsequent anaesthetics in patients with an electronic difficult airway alert in two hospitals. The alert was displayed in the anaesthetic record in 88 percent of cases, but documented as read before induction in only 54 percent. Alerts were missed more often out of hours and when the patient was transferred from another hospital. Anaesthetists reported alert fatigue from other electronic warnings. Documentation of reading the alert may underestimate how often it was actually seen. Alerts were displayed less often for patients transferred in, because records from other hospitals did not carry them.

records.title: Unanticipated difficult tracheal intubation after a documented difficult airway: frequency and consequences
records.abstract: In a regional database of 2,030 patients with a documented difficult tracheal intubation, we reviewed the next airway management within five years. Difficulty was unanticipated in 31 percent of cases, and unanticipated cases more often involved multiple attempts, desaturation below 80 percent and emergency front-of-neck access. Unanticipated difficulty was commoner in emergency settings and in patients treated at a different hospital from the index event. The database relied on voluntary reporting and probably missed some events. Patients whose difficulty was unanticipated were more often older and admitted as emergencies.

records.title: Do patients know? Awareness of difficult airway status and use of alert letters
records.abstract: We telephoned 180 patients who had been sent a difficult airway letter between 6 and 36 months earlier. Forty percent could say that they had a difficult airway and 22 percent reported carrying the letter or an alert card. Awareness was lower in older patients, patients with limited English and patients whose index anaesthetic had been an emergency. Several patients said the letter used technical language they did not understand. The response rate was 61 percent. Patients who had discussed the letter with their GP were more likely to know their status.

records.title: Using a hospital difficult airway database for research: completeness and linkage to later anaesthetics
records.abstract: We compared a hospital's difficult airway database with a manual review of anaesthetic records over two years. The database captured 76 percent of events meeting its own definition, with lower capture for events outside theatres. Linkage of database entries to later anaesthetics in the same hospital succeeded for 90 percent using the hospital number. Anaesthetics in other hospitals were invisible to the database. The authors recommend reporting capture rates alongside any outcome derived from such databases. Capture improved after a reporting prompt was added to the anaesthetic record in the second year.

records.title: Interrupted time series for evaluating hospital safety interventions: pitfalls with few data points and concurrent changes
records.abstract: We re-analysed 42 published interrupted time series of hospital safety interventions. Twenty-six had fewer than eight data points on one side of the change, and 19 did not mention concurrent interventions. Re-analysis with autocorrelation and seasonality taken into account changed the conclusion in 11 studies. We recommend at least eight points before and after, a pre-specified model, a control series where possible, and an explicit list of co-interventions with their dates. Studies with a control series were less likely to change conclusion on re-analysis, but only five of the 42 used one.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Alert systems make known difficulty available at the next anaesthetic in roughly half to four fifths of patients, but presence is not recognition: one study found alerts displayed in 88 percent and documented as read in 54 percent. Difficulty is unanticipated in about three in ten next airway managements after a documented difficult intubation. Hospital airway databases miss about a quarter of events, and time series of safety interventions are often too short and confounded by co-interventions. The national 34 percent figure recalled by the model is a lead with an unverified identifier, not a retrieved record, and it was not appraised.
response.gradeRationale: Single-centre before-after and observational studies with concurrent changes and incomplete databases; consistent direction but serious risk of bias.

The untraced national figure appears only as an unverified lead.

response.overview: Retrospective segmented time series of recognition of known airway difficulty before later airway management, January 2019 to August 2026, using the difficult airway database linked to anaesthetic records and incident reports.
response.population: Patients registered in the difficult airway database who had a later airway management episode (anaesthetic or emergency intubation) in the hospital; the first later episode per patient per quarter is counted.
response.exposure: Airway management after 1 March 2023, when the wristband, electronic alert and letter were in place, compared with the pre-existing trend.
response.procedures: Two trainees review the anaesthetic record of each later episode using a tested form: whether the alert was present, whether known difficulty was documented as recognised before airway management, the airway plan, and whether difficulty was unanticipated. A random 15 percent are reviewed by both trainees. Database capture is checked against a manual review of one year's anaesthetic records. Co-interventions (training, equipment, guidelines) are listed with dates.

response.designSummary: Segmented regression of quarterly proportions, 17 quarters before and 14 after the change.
response.sampleSize: About 400 later episodes give about 12 per quarter, 200 before and 200 after. With recognition near 45 percent before and 70 percent after, a two-period comparison would have more than 95 percent power, but the segmented model is less precise: with 17 and 14 quarterly points and moderate autocorrelation, a level change of 20 percentage points is detectable with about 80 percent power. A change of 10 points would not be distinguishable from noise.
response.primaryAnalysis: Segmented binomial regression of quarterly recognition with terms for pre-existing trend, level change and slope change at March 2023, with autocorrelation checked and a pre-specified model.
response.secondaryAnalysis: The same model for unanticipated difficulty; alert presence described; recognition by emergency status, age band and language where recorded.
response.missingData: Episodes with missing anaesthetic records are counted and reported; not imputed.
response.multiplicity: One primary outcome; secondary outcomes reported with intervals.

response.title: Recognition of known difficult airway before later airway management after introduction of a wristband and electronic alert system: a retrospective segmented time series
response.abstract: Objective: to assess whether a difficult airway alert system changed documented recognition of known difficulty before later airway management. Design: retrospective segmented time series, January 2019 to August 2026, from a hospital difficult airway database linked to anaesthetic records. Results will be reported after analysis.
response.introduction: Alert systems aim to ensure that the next anaesthetist knows about a patient's difficult airway, but alerts can be displayed without being read.
response.methods: Later airway management episodes were identified from the database and reviewed for documented recognition, alert presence and unanticipated difficulty. Quarterly proportions were analysed with segmented regression, listing co-interventions and reporting database capture.
response.results: No records have been reviewed yet. The report will present episodes per quarter, recognition before and after the change, unanticipated difficulty and database capture.
response.discussion: The discussion will interpret any change against co-interventions and database capture and will not cite the untraced national figure.
response.limitations: Co-interventions, documentation of recognition, and episodes outside the hospital.
response.summary: RECORD-structured draft with results left empty.
